description: Within this cluster of 24 articles, the exploration of crowdsourcing spans innovation, health research, and crowdsourcing definition. Different perspectives on defining crowdsourcing are presented (Estellés-Arolas & GonzálezLadrón-de-Guevara, 2012; Saxton et al., 2013). The articles presented examine innovation applications, with Hutter et al. (2011) stressing the synergy of competition and cooperation for optimal idea quality. Health research discussions range from general insights (Ranard et al., 2014; Swan, 2012) to specific applications, like emotional responses to the COVID-19 pandemic (Barzilay et al., 2020).

Comprising 17 articles, the green cluster shifts focus to data generation via crowdsourcing. Micro-tasks on digital platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, annotation outsourcing (Patterson et al., 2014; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019), and diverse data creation tasks, from emotion lexicons (Mohammad & Turney, 2012) to algorithm training through sketching (Sangkloy et al., 2016), indicate the versatility of crowdsourced data dynamics.

With 14 articles, the blue cluster explores crowdsourcing’s role in generating geographic data and aiding disaster response. Topics include geospatial data collection (Heipke, 2010), addressing data quality concerns (See et al., 2016), enhancing global land cover maps (Fritz et al., 2009), and leveraging crowdsourced information for disaster events (Crooks et al., 2012). Despite data quality challenges, Goodchild and Glennon (2010) argue for the benefits of crowdsourced data in crises.

Comprising 14 articles, the yellow cluster leverages crowdsourcing for research data. Ensuring high-quality data is predominant (Behrend et al., 2011; Steelman et al., 2014), with topics ranging from Amazon Mechanical Turk’s suitability for behavioral research (Crump et al., 2013) to the influence of workers’ reputations on data quality (Peer et al., 2014). The cluster also suggests flexible platforms for managing Amazon Mechanical Turk studies (Litman et al., 2017). Positioned at a noticeable distance from the main clusters, this cluster shares fewer references with other groups and emphasizes issues such as data quality, platform suitability, and research design. This reflects its unique methodological and topical contribution and signals an underexplored but important area within gig economy research.

With 14 articles, the purple cluster explores the well-being of gig workers, examining aspects like precarity, insecurity, and the influence of algorithms (Friedman, 2014; Graham et al., 2017; Kalleberg, 2009; Rosenblat & Stark, 2016; Wood et al., 2019).

The orange cluster contains five articles and explores the challenges and solutions in mobile crowdsourcing. Discussions include smartphone utilization (Chatzimilioudis et al., 2012) and issues on motivating user participation (Feng et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2012).
